result: Among long COVID participants at 6-8 months, 5/97 (JHU) and 51/281 (LIINC) met IOM ME/CFS criteria and 2/97 and 29/281 met CCC, mapped retrospectively from non-ME/CFS-specific data; ME/CFS cases were more often female with more symptoms.
reason: Reports the share of long COVID meeting ME/CFS criteria with no uninfected comparison, so it cannot replicate the infected-vs-uninfected incidence; it adds cohort estimates like the Dehlia detail.

result: In 261 ME/CFS vs 165 controls (MCAM, 7 sites), CogState accuracy did not differ but processing speed was slower at most of 5 timepoints (d 0.3-0.5); a clinic day worsened performance, but maximal cycle exercise did not further slow it.
reason: Same measures as the finding: it replicates the processing-speed deficit (smaller effect than claimed) and adds a time course. It does not support the post-exercise worsening part of the claim, which should be noted.

result: Maximal cycle exercise did not further reduce CogState speed in 182 ME/CFS vs 160 controls, although the full clinic day did worsen cognition.
reason: No imaging, and the finding is Cook's fMRI exertion design. The behavioural exercise null is captured under the neuro-cognition link.

result: In a Mayo long COVID survey (247 LC responders vs 40 infected controls; 34% and 50% response), questionnaire-screened generalized joint hypermobility was more common in LC (p=0.026 as far as the truncated abstract shows), and 58% vs 0% screened positive for ME/CFS.
reason: This is a long COVID version of the hypermobility overlap, like Lubell in the detail. Evidence is weak: self-report screen, low response, small control group, truncated numbers.

result: 58% of 247 long COVID survey responders screened positive for ME/CFS vs 0% of 40 infected controls without LC; orthostatic intolerance questionnaire score averaged 4.0 vs 0.
reason: It reports only a self-reported orthostatic intolerance score, with no formal POTS testing or cerebral blood flow measure. Its ME/CFS-screen result fits the post-COVID ME/CFS finding better, as weak clinic-survey evidence.

result: Meta-analysis of 12 studies (2,665 patients) found a pooled PEM prevalence of 55% (95% CI 38-71%) in post-acute COVID syndrome at 3 months or more; DSQ-PEM was the most used of 7 instruments.
reason: The newer atlas finding lc-pem-prevalence covers PEM prevalence in long COVID; this pooled estimate supports it. Check that it is not already cited.

result: In MCAM (595 ME/CFS vs 328 controls), 76% vs 17.4% had at least one chronic overlapping pain condition: migraine/headache 48.1%, fibromyalgia 45.0% (PR 147.7), low back pain 33.1% (PR 39.5), IBS 31.6%.
reason: This is clinical comorbidity prevalence, not genetic correlation or colocalisation, so it does not test the genetics finding. No clinical pain-comorbidity finding exists; it could be a new-finding candidate. The IBS part is linked under gut-ibs-overlap.

result: IBS was present in 31.6% of 595 ME/CFS patients in the 7-site MCAM cohort, among 76% with at least one overlapping pain condition vs 17.4% of controls.
reason: An independent multisite cohort measuring IBS prevalence, close to the pooled 37%. The abstract does not give the IBS-specific ratio vs controls.

result: In 50,115 Danish residents (25,249 test-positive vs 24,866 test-negative, mostly vaccinated), infection was linked to a 3% higher fatigue score (SR 1.03) and higher odds of PEM (OR 2.04, 1.81-2.30) 2-18 months later; hospitalisation raised fatigue scores 23%; prior psychiatric conditions did not modify risk.
reason: It measures fatigue scores and DSQ PEM against test-negative controls, not ME/CFS criteria or the course of criteria-defined cases. It fits best as population evidence of excess PEM after infection.

result: In 83 neurological long COVID vs 22 recovered controls, global cognition was lower (OCLz -0.39 vs +0.32), 48% had episodic memory deficits, cortex was thinner in left posterior superior temporal gyrus, and FA was lower and RD higher across widespread white matter, correlating with cognition.
reason: It reports no thalamus, basal ganglia or choroid plexus findings. Its main result is widespread white-matter diffusion change linked to cognition, which is a long COVID version of the white-matter finding.
